question: How can a melody sing above a busy accompaniment?
intro: A short étude that asks for weight as well as speed: the right-hand melody is projected in octaves over widely spaced left-hand figures. Listen for the quieter middle and the heavier return of the opening.

sections.label: Intensified return · approximate
sections.mNote: opening melody now projected above triplet chords in both hands

relations.label: The octave melody returns
relations.basis: The A′ section intensifies the opening D♯-minor material after the quieter middle. These excerpts compare a phrase from the first section with its return inside the section marked near 64 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.930, sustained 12 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 51 s (cache/form/scriabin-etude-op8-12.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A line above the activity
cues.text: Try following the melody as one continuing line, rather than giving every accompanying note equal attention. The study asks the pianist to keep that line distinct while covering wide distances on the keyboard.
cues.evidence: The score outline describes a chordal melody above a widely spaced accompaniment. This cue concerns the texture, not an individual note or hand movement at a precise second: https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tude_op._8_no_12_de_Scriabine
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A publisher’s support
cues.text: Mitrofan Belyayev heard Scriabin’s music in 1894 and began publishing his works and paying advances. Their surviving correspondence records not just encouragement but negotiations over deadlines and revisions.
cues.evidence: Valentina Rubcova’s Henle preface recounts Belyayev’s support from 1894 and quotes the correspondence: https://www.henle.de/media/56/3c/dd/1697725817/1486-1697725817-sync.pdf

cues.title: Quieter does not mean still
cues.text: Across the quieter middle, listen for how much motion remains beneath the melody. A reduction in force can change the character even when the accompaniment continues to keep the hands busy.
cues.evidence: The recorded level falls across roughly 0:35–0:45, but the analysis continues to detect frequent attacks. The cue does not depend on an automatically estimated key.

cues.title: An étude revised before publication
cues.text: Scriabin was still revising the Op. 8 studies in March 1895. He also sent Belyayev a second version of the D♯ minor étude but asked him not to publish it immediately. The collection appeared in July that year.
cues.evidence: Rubcova quotes Scriabin’s 1895 letters about the revisions and withheld alternative, and dates publication to 6/18 July 1895. This does not identify the edition used in this performance: https://www.henle.de/media/56/3c/dd/1697725817/1486-1697725817-sync.pdf

cues.title: A stronger return
cues.text: Compare this later, more forceful stretch with the opening. Can you still follow the melody through the accompanying activity, and does the extra weight change where the phrase seems to be heading?
cues.evidence: The analysis finds a higher recorded level and more frequent attacks around 1:05–1:25 than in the opening. These measurements support the broad contrast, not a claim about an exact thematic entrance.

cues.title: Students at the White House
cues.text: Awadagin Pratt took part in the White House classical-music workshop and concert on 4 November 2009. This recording is an extract from the event’s video, which also documents performances by students.
cues.evidence: The archived White House video page dates the event, names Pratt and describes the workshop and concert: https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/photos-and-video/video/white-house-workshop-classical-music

cues.title: The attacks spread out
cues.text: Across the closing gestures, compare the spaces between attacks with the denser movement earlier in the study. Notice how the sound can continue between notes even as the activity diminishes.
cues.evidence: The report shows fewer detected attacks and a falling recorded level around 1:40–1:55. It does not identify the later sound at the end of this live recording, so no claim of final silence is made.

transitions.title: The octave line relaxes, the triplets continue
transitions.how: The forceful D♯-minor statement opens into the relative-major region, F♯ major, and the melody loses some of its octave-driven weight. The left hand does not stop: its widely spaced triplet figures keep a moving foundation beneath the more restrained right-hand phrase. The two regions share the F♯ and A♯ of their tonic triads, so the change can sound like a release inside one tonal world rather than a wholly new beginning.
transitions.evidence: The Quieter middle boundary is 0:36, a strong novelty peak; relative level drops around 0:35–0:45 while attacks continue. The score supplies the relative-major turn and continuing triplet accompaniment. Shared tonic-triad notes describe the key relationship, not a claimed single pivot chord; the report’s enharmonic E♭ labels do not change the written D♯ spelling.

transitions.title: The melody now shares its hand with chords
transitions.how: The middle’s chromatic continuation gathers force and restores the opening D♯-minor melody. Scriabin changes the mechanism underneath it: triplet chords now occupy both hands, so the right hand must project the longer melodic notes while also contributing to the accompaniment. Low bass notes and a thicker middle register increase the weight without replacing the tune. The return is intensified by added simultaneous work, not merely by playing the opening louder.
transitions.evidence: The Intensified return boundary is 1:04, with novelty at 1:00 and 1:04 and the highest relative-level window at 1:05. The relations file matches 21.5–33.5 s with 72.5–84.5 s. The changed two-hand triplet texture is described from the score at https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tude_op._8_no_12_de_Scriabine; the match itself does not separate the hands.

transitions.title: Continuous figuration becomes separated final chords
transitions.how: The enlarged melody gives way to a final ascent shared by both hands, then to separated chords. Scriabin exchanges continuous triplet accompaniment for cadential punctuation: the pianist no longer has to keep a singing line suspended over ceaseless motion. D♯ minor remains the destination, with D♯–F♯–A♯ confirming the tonic rather than changing it to major. The spaces around the last chords make their attacks and remaining resonance distinct parts of the close.
transitions.evidence: The Closing gestures boundary is 1:44, a novelty peak; attacks become fewer and relative level falls across 1:40–1:55. The score supplies the two-hand ascent and concluding chords. The live recording contains later sound that the analysis cannot identify, so this describes musical closure rather than claiming final silence.

composer.epithet: A pianist who replaced the need for a resolving tonic with recurring harmonic fields, accelerating figures and carefully organised light.
facts: Moscow Conservatory, 1888–92; piano with Vasily Safonov, composition studies with Taneyev and Arensky
Piano at the Moscow Conservatory from 1898; left regular teaching in 1903
Mitrofan Belyayev; later Serge Koussevitzky, who conducted the premiere of Prometheus
Ten numbered piano sonatas, preludes and études; three numbered symphonies, a piano concerto and two large orchestral poems
composer.background:
Scriabin was born in Moscow into a family whose musical and military occupations coexisted. His mother, Lyubov, a trained pianist, died while he was an infant; his father’s diplomatic career left much of his upbringing to female relatives. He attended a cadet school while pursuing music, then entered the Moscow Conservatory in 1888. Rachmaninoff was a fellow student. Scriabin studied piano with Vasily Safonov and theoretical subjects with Sergei Taneyev and Anton Arensky, graduating as a pianist in 1892 with the full composition course unfinished. His earliest published music identifies the piano as both instrument and compositional laboratory.

Chopin supplied recognisable genres: prelude, étude, mazurka, nocturne and impromptu. Scriabin’s Twenty-four Preludes, Op. 11, traverse all major and minor keys in the order familiar from Chopin’s Op. 28. The influence extends to melody floating over an independently patterned accompaniment and to chromatic notes that delay a cadence. An injury to his right hand during his student years made the distribution of work between the hands a practical concern. The Prelude and Nocturne for the left hand, Op. 9, create melody, bass and harmonic filling within the reach of one hand.
